title: The path of dhamma
hook: a collection of the Buddha's verses, beloved across the Buddhist world (Dhammapada)
tomorrow: if everyone dies, why does it say the earnest never do?

segments.voice: Yesterday, slow reading: a few lines, three times, then quiet. Three times. Today that slow pace meets its first book, and the book's first line.

A stranger bumps your arm on the train and your coffee hits the floor. Before anyone says sorry, you're already reading their face: did they mean it? That snap read of intent is where the Dhammapada begins. Its very first line, in Max Müller's translation: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." Mind first. And Buddhist tradition hangs a story on that line, about a blind monk, a rainy night, and a path covered in insects.
screen: `COFFEE ON THE FLOOR. DID THEY MEAN IT?` → `ALL THAT WE ARE…` → `A BLIND MONK, A RAINY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Dhammapada is a small book of the Buddha's verses, and its old commentary gives each verse a story. The first belongs to an elder named Cakkhupala. Tradition says he vowed to spend a rainy season without lying down, only walking and sitting in meditation. His eyes failed, and he kept walking. One night after rain, insects swarmed onto his walking path, and he crushed them without seeing. In the morning, visiting monks found the bodies and went to the Buddha: this monk is killing living things. The Buddha asked: did you see him kill them? No. Neither did he. He had no thought of killing, so there was no fault. Then the verses. The first chapter is the Twin-Verses, lines in pairs. Act with an evil thought, and "pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage." Act with a pure thought, and happiness follows like a shadow. So the teaching: in Buddhism, karma is intention. In another sutta the Buddha says it outright: intention is what he calls karma. That's why Buddhists start with the mind, and why the same act can weigh differently depending on what was meant. It isn't think-positive. A smile over a cruel plan still pulls the cart. One more thing worth telling a friend: some readers take the title two ways, verses of dhamma or the path of dhamma, hearing pada as a line or as a step.
screen: `A BLIND MONK ON A RAINY PATH.` · `NO INTENTION, NO FAULT.` · `THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.` · `KARMA IS INTENTION.` · then, large: `THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap. Before you move one finger, notice the wish to move it, then let the finger lift and settle. Do it a few times, slowly, catching the intention each time before the motion. Then let the hands rest, and stay quiet for the rest of the sit.
The path of dhamma: the Dhammapada, the Buddha's verses, where each line is a step and the first step is the mind.
For the road: the path, with the mind walking first on it. The Dhammapada is open.

howItsDone: Buddhists in many countries read, chant and memorize verses of the Dhammapada; teachers often tell the commentary's story behind a verse before explaining it.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3: written new in recipe v3. Shape story: the commentary's story of the elder Cakkhupala (verse 1) is the scene; the teaching named plainly is that in Buddhism karma is intention (AN 6.63, paraphrased). The hook answers day 1428's question (what is the very first thing the Dhammapada says?).

Check Müller 1881 verse 1 word for word: 'All that we are is the result of what we have thought' and 'pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.' Verse 2 is paraphrased (happiness follows like a shadow). Müller's first chapter title is 'The Twin-Verses'; confirm.

Cakkhupala story paraphrased from the Dhammapada commentary (vow not to lie down for a rains retreat, blindness, insects crushed on the walking path, the Buddha: no intention, no fault). The commentary's past-life part (he had once blinded someone as a physician) is left out for length; a Buddhist Keeper may want it as the 'wheel follows' half.

'pada can mean a step or a line of verse' follows standard Pali dictionaries (PTS: foot, step, path; also a line of verse); confirm. Gloss 'Pali: the language of the Theravada scriptures' is a general description; confirm.
Original धम्मपद is Pali in Devanagari letters; confirm spelling and the sound-out.
howItsDone says Buddhists 'in many countries' read and chant the Dhammapada and that teachers 'often' tell the commentary story; this is general and unsourced: soften or cut if a Keeper prefers.
